Even so, Yemen did not lose its distinct character as an agricultural country. Centuries of farming had given its people rich practical experience in reducing their complete dependence on natural conditions.

When we look at agricultural activity elsewhere in Arabia during the same period, we find similar practices and accumulated experience. Agriculture existed not only in Yemen, but also in Ḥaḍramawt, Oman in the south-east, al-Yamāma in the east, the Ḥijāz in the north, Tihāma in the west—both its northern and southern parts—and the many oases along desert routes and inside the desert itself, even in the volcanic regions known as the ḥarrāt.

Across all these regions, groups of Arabs worked the land. Some were permanently settled, while others were only partly settled. They used underground water and seasonal surface water through methods that were relatively advanced for their time.

They farmed not only to meet their own immediate needs but also to produce goods for exchange. These products reached not only small local markets but also the larger markets that served the peninsula as a whole, as the historical sources mentioned earlier tell us.
Those sources sometimes give details about the range of agricultural products brought to these markets. Some of them had even been processed in ways that involved a degree of manufacturing.

Faced with this evidence, the modern researcher can only regret that medieval Arab-Islamic historians who wrote about the pre-Islamic period give us no figures, even rough ones, for the amount of land under cultivation in the different parts of Arabia. Nor do they give us enough information to estimate how many people worked this land compared with the total population of the peninsula.
This makes it very difficult to reach a firm scientific conclusion about how much agriculture shaped the economic structure and the direction in which it was developing.
More importantly, it makes it difficult to know how strongly agriculture affected the social structure of Arabia as a whole, or of western Arabia—where the Ḥijāz lies—in particular.

When it comes to trade, however, we have more historical evidence to work with. Early historians give us enough information about commercial activity to form a clearer picture: its economic and social effects on the population, the reach of its foreign connections, and the scale of the profits made by the leaders of Mecca, especially the leaders of Quraysh.

By the end of the sixth century CE, these men had come to dominate trade between the Arabian Peninsula and the outside world. In doing so, they became an important force in pushing the relationship between productive work and commerce toward a growing contradiction, as we shall see.
Craft production: Before drawing conclusions from what we have seen so far, we also need to ask what place handicrafts held in the economic structure of pre-Islamic society.

Where had crafts reached in the development of the economy—or, more precisely, in the development of the division of labour? And what was their relationship to commodity production during this period?
The answer helps us identify the historical stage that Arab society had reached in the late Jāhiliyya.
The simple existence of handicrafts is not enough. What matters is their relationship to agriculture.
Were crafts still carried out as part of agricultural life, or had they separated from farming and become independent occupations in their own right?
These two situations belong to two different stages of development.

When handicrafts are still part of the work done by farming communities, society is at an earlier stage in the division of labour. The later stage begins when some people become full-time craftsmen while others remain farmers.

This second stage is more advanced because such a division means that society has reached a point where people can produce more than they need for their own immediate daily survival. Production is becoming social production for exchange—in other words, commodity production. Its products can now enter trade.
At this stage, trade becomes a social activity that interacts positively with productive work.

The separation of handicrafts from agriculture is therefore an important sign of development. It marks a new stage in the history of ancient societies. It is a form of specialization in productive work. This usually brings greater productivity, gives human labour greater power to transform nature, creates new craft skills, and encourages improvements in technique.
This separation of handicrafts from agriculture—and their development into production for exchange—had in fact already taken place by the end of the Jāhiliyya.

Whenever the Arabic sources mention these crafts, they speak of their products as things that were exchanged, bought, and sold. They also speak of markets for them, and even of markets specializing in particular crafts, such as the goldsmiths’ market in Yathrib, later Medina.
It is particularly significant for our argument that weapons were among the goods manufactured in Mecca at this time. Other Meccan crafts included pottery and the making of beds and couches.
Some of the people who worked in these crafts—especially metalworking—were also well-known figures in the history of Islam’s beginnings.

Al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra and al-ʿĀṣ ibn Hishām, the brother of Abū Jahl, were both blacksmiths. Umayya ibn Khalaf al-Jumaḥī worked in pottery, while ʿUtba ibn Abī Waqqāṣ was a carpenter. All of these men fought against Islam at Badr or Uḥud.
Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ made and sharpened arrows, while Khabbāb ibn al-Aratt was a swordsmith. Both supported Islam.
There were also the well-known crafts of al-Ṭāʾif, each with its own markets. These included tanning, charcoal-making, extracting tar, and distilling wine, among others.
Yemen was famous for the quality of its crafts, especially weapons and textiles. Yathrib also produced metal goods such as jewellery and ornaments, as well as weapons.
As we said, the existence of weapons production in Mecca itself is especially significant.
First, because of the particular nature of Mecca’s economy. Mecca was not an agricultural town. It lay in what the Qurʾān calls “a valley without cultivation.”

Craft production in Mecca therefore could not have existed as a branch of farming. It had to stand on its own. This means it had already moved beyond household craft work intended simply to meet immediate personal needs and had entered the stage of production for exchange.
Second, the particular presence of blacksmithing in Mecca deserves our attention.
The relatively advanced use of iron at this time is itself a historical development with a specific meaning in Marxist social analysis.
As we have just seen, blacksmithing was a common occupation. Even men of high standing within Quraysh, such as al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra and al-ʿĀṣ ibn Hishām, were associated with it.

Are we really to suppose that blacksmiths produced weapons but no agricultural tools, at a time when rising agricultural productivity was already attracting wealthy Qurayshi merchants from Mecca to invest part of their money in agricultural land at al-Ṭāʾif?
We also know for a fact that iron ploughs existed during this period of Arab history, both before Islam and around the time Islam emerged.

There is another point as well. Some modern Arab writers have argued that Quraysh became so absorbed in trade, and grew so wealthy from it, that they lost interest in warfare. Some other Arabs even mocked them for this and came to look down on them.

There may be some exaggeration in this view, but its basic point is sound. Trade was the main concern of Quraysh in Mecca because it formed the foundation of the city’s economy and the chief source of wealth for its leaders.

This fact shaped the other forms of productive work in Mecca, especially handicrafts. Their main purpose became production for exchange. This applied even to weapons production, as well as to the other branches of blacksmithing, metalworking, goldsmithing, and related crafts.

Belyaev was therefore right to conclude that the Arabs of the Jāhiliyya had already moved beyond a division of labour between cultivators and livestock herders and had reached a later stage in which society was divided between craftsmen and farmers.
He writes that, at this later stage,

Arab crafts were not limited to pottery and weaving—fields in which they had reached a high level. They also worked with smelted metals. Iron was available in the territory of the Sulaym tribe, east of Medina, which became so well known for ironworking that its neighbours called it the tribe of the qayns, or blacksmiths. They were also known for smelting and refining iron (...) Farmers used a variety of iron tools, including iron ploughshares.
Forms of slavery: The surviving accounts of the Jāhiliyya agree that slavery was not foreign to this part of the ancient world.

The forms of slavery we can see in the late Jāhiliyya suggest that the institution already had a long history in Arabia. But we do not have documents that tell us when it began or what forms it had taken in earlier periods.
For the period we are studying, however, the historical evidence clearly shows that slavery had a place in the social and economic structure.
Slaves were used as a productive force, not merely as objects of consumption.

We know that slaves were used for domestic work by the leaders of Quraysh in Mecca, by wealthy people in other towns, and in the households of tribal and clan chiefs. Slaves were also themselves a common and widely traded “commodity.”

But their role went beyond domestic service and trade. Slaves—especially Abyssinians—were also used in productive work such as agriculture, including irrigation, as well as in crafts and livestock raising. Some were also employed in commercial work.
Even so, the use of slaves as a productive force is not enough to conclude that slave relations of production were the dominant form of production in pre-Islamic society.
There are several reasons for this.

First, slave labour was not the main element within the productive forces. This was true in the urban and semi-urban economy as well as in the Bedouin economy based on herding and livestock raising. Free people made up a substantial part of the productive population, at least as large as the enslaved part.

Second, more slaves were used as household servants, guards, or goods traded between local and foreign markets than were used directly as productive labour. Their role as producers was therefore neither their main role nor the dominant one.

Many were Abyssinians of Ethiopian or Sudanese origin. Some were white Persians or Romans who had originally been taken prisoner during wars between the Persian and Byzantine empires and were later brought into Arabia for sale.
Foreign slaves in Arab society were therefore usually acquired through trade rather than directly through war.
Arab captives who became slaves after intertribal wars were much fewer in number than foreign slaves. The reason was that Arab prisoners taken in tribal wars were usually freed in one of two ways.
Either their tribe launched a counterattack against the tribe holding them, or a ransom was paid for their release.

There was another factor as well. In pre-Islamic custom, being taken prisoner could bring shame on both the captive and the captive’s tribe. Some people were even said to prefer killing themselves rather than being captured.

For all these reasons, Arab captives generally became slaves only when no one could pay their ransom and they could not ransom themselves. In that case, they could be bought and sold or put to work in productive or non-productive activities.
But, as we have already noted, these forms of work were not carried out by slaves alone.

In short, slavery in Arabia had its own particular form. Within each tribe, slaves were mostly foreigners, followed by people from other Arab tribes, while the members of the tribe itself remained free despite the differences in wealth and living conditions among them.

The Bedouin economy: We do not have enough precise historical evidence to measure the role of the Bedouin economy against the settled economy of agriculture, trade, and craft production. We have already noted this problem.
Even so, the evidence that survives allows us to form a general picture.

The first point to make is that the importance of either type of economy cannot be judged simply by its size. What matters most is how strongly it affected the direction in which the whole economy of the late Jāhiliyya was developing.

There is no doubt that Bedouin Arabs outnumbered the people of towns and settled communities. Nor is there any doubt that their main means of living was livestock raising, especially camels. The economic return from this way of life may in itself have been considerable.
But its defining feature was its almost complete dependence on natural conditions: the climate, the timing of rainfall, the location of pasture, and so on.

Human beings had little control over these conditions apart from the ability to move from one place to another. Even that movement was not really a matter of choice. It was forced on them by the search for suitable weather and pasture, and whatever suitability they found was temporary.
This dependence on nature was both a weakness and a constraint. It helped keep the Bedouin economy relatively underdeveloped.

The tribal social system created further pressures that drained and reduced its resources. These included tribal wars, such as blood feuds, armed struggles over pasture or its protection, and the economic burden of maintaining armed nomadic groups.
The settled economy was moving in the opposite direction.
The forces driving agriculture, trade, and craft production were not only helping the settled economy grow. They were also beginning to influence the Bedouin economy itself.

Over time, the Bedouin economy could lose its earlier historical role and become drawn into the new process of development. In other words, it would increasingly come under the same forces shaping the settled economy, to the extent required by the wider laws of social development under the particular conditions of pre-Islamic Arabia.
The continuing interaction among the three main parts of the settled economy—agriculture, trade, and handicrafts that had become independent of agriculture—was gradually becoming stronger.
This gave the settled economy the decisive role in the new historical development of the economic structure of pre-Islamic society as a whole.

The old structure had been based mainly on a natural economy and primitive communal ownership. It was now moving toward a structure based on commodity production and private ownership of the means of production.
This transformation was already taking place objectively during the period we are studying, though at a relatively slow pace.

It meant that the settled economy, through its own forms of growth and development, was beginning to create the material and productive basis for a society divided into classes rather than one divided into scattered tribal units.
4 — The Direction of Change in the Social Structure
The direction of economic development described above appeared in a number of visible social changes. These allow us to see more clearly where that development was historically leading.
At the same time, these changes contained the beginnings of a contradiction between the developing economy and the social structure of the old, primitive tribal system.
In an earlier period, the level and forms of social life in Arabia had broadly matched the level of economic life.

That balance began to change when activity returned to the land and sea trade routes connecting Arabia—especially its western regions—with countries that were economically more advanced than the Arabian interior, including China, India, Persia, Syria, and the coast of East Africa.
This renewed contact with the outside world gave Arabia an important role as an international commercial middleman.
That role, in turn, pushed tribal leaders—especially the leaders of Quraysh—to move beyond simply providing a route for trade. They began taking a direct part in trade themselves.
This had an important economic effect. It began to separate the leaders of the clans of Mecca, especially those of Quraysh, from the leaders of tribes living away from the major trade routes.
Here we can see the beginnings of an economic divide that was bound to create a social divide as well.
The first difference was between regions that gained little or nothing from international trade and commercial brokerage and those that profited from both.

The second arose within the prosperous regions themselves: between their wealthy leaders on one side, and the poorer members of their own clans and the smaller tribes tied to them through loyalty and alliance on the other.
These early forms of economic and social inequality created a contradiction between an economic structure moving toward a new stage of development and a social structure that was lagging behind it.
